title: 2 Chronicles 9:1–12
context: 2 Chronicles 9:1–12 is kept whole. The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame and comes to test him with hard questions, bringing a great caravan of spices, gold, and precious stones. Solomon answers all her questions, and seeing his wisdom, his house, his table, and his ascent to the LORD’s house, she is overwhelmed. She says the report was true and that she had not heard half of it, and she blesses the LORD, who loved Israel and made Solomon king to do justice and righteousness. She gives lavish gifts, Huram’s and Solomon’s servants bring algum wood and precious stones, and Solomon gives her all she desires before she returns home. The parallel in 1 Kings 10:1–13 follows the same order with small differences: Kings spells the wood almug and says it was used for pillars, while Chronicles says terraces, and the two describe Solomon’s gifts to her in different words. Consistent with the drafted notes on 1 Kings 10, both traditions read the queen’s praise as a Gentile’s acknowledgment of the LORD’s gifts to Solomon, and Jesus later refers to her (Matthew 12:42).

verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to test Solomon with hard questions at Jerusalem, with a very great caravan, including camels that bore spices, gold in abundance, and precious stones. When she had come to Solomon, she talked with him about all that was in her heart.
verses.arminianNotes: The queen of Sheba hears of Solomon’s fame and comes with a great caravan to test him with hard questions, talking with him about all that was in her heart. Arminian readers see a sincere seeker drawn by Solomon’s wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God drawing a Gentile ruler to the wisdom he gave Solomon. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:1, and they hold the location of Sheba, often associated with southwestern Arabia, with caution.

verses.text: Solomon answered all her questions. There wasn’t anything hidden from Solomon which he didn’t tell her.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon answers all her questions, and nothing is hidden from him. Arminians see the fulfillment of God’s promise to give Solomon wisdom (2 Chronicles 1:11–12), shown publicly before a foreign ruler.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress that Solomon’s wisdom is God’s gift. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the wisdom God gives and its witness to others.

verses.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,
verses.arminianNotes: The queen sees Solomon’s wisdom and the house he built. Arminian readers see wisdom shown not only in words but also in visible works, which confirm what she had heard.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the visible order of Solomon’s kingdom as evidence of God’s blessing. Both traditions read the verse as building toward the queen’s response.

verses.text: the food of his table, the seating of his servants, the attendance of his ministers, their clothing, his cup bearers and their clothing, and his ascent by which he went up to the LORD’s house, there was no more spirit in her.
verses.arminianNotes: She sees his table, servants, ministers, cupbearers, and his ascent to the LORD’s house, and there is no more spirit in her. Arminians see the queen overwhelmed by the order and splendor of a kingdom blessed by God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the phrase can also mean she was breathless. Both traditions note that Chronicles mentions Solomon’s ascent to the LORD’s house, which keeps the temple in view.

verses.text: She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts and of your wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes: She tells Solomon the report she heard in her own land of his acts and wisdom was true. Arminian readers see a seeker whose doubts are answered by seeing for herself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God confirming his word through what she saw. Both traditions read the verse as an honest acknowledgment of the truth of what she had heard, which is shared ground.

verses.text: However I didn’t believe their words until I came, and my eyes had seen it; and behold half of the greatness of your wisdom wasn’t told me. You exceed the fame that I heard!
verses.arminianNotes: She says she did not believe until she came and saw, and half of his wisdom had not been told her. Arminians see the reality surpassing the report, which encourages honest inquiry into God’s works.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as showing the abundance of God’s gifts. Both traditions note that Jesus refers to the queen coming to hear Solomon’s wisdom and says that one greater than Solomon is present (Matthew 12:42).

verses.text: Happy are your men, and happy are these your servants, who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom.
verses.arminianNotes: She calls Solomon’s men and servants happy, because they stand before him continually and hear his wisdom. Arminian readers see the blessing of living near wisdom and learning from it day by day.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as praise for the gift of wise leadership. Both traditions read the verse as part of the queen’s recognition of God’s blessing on Solomon’s court.

verses.text: Blessed be the LORD your God, who delighted in you and set you on his throne to be king for the LORD your God, because your God loved Israel, to establish them forever. Therefore he made you king over them, to do justice and righteousness.”
verses.arminianNotes: She blesses the LORD, who delighted in Solomon and set him on his throne as king for the LORD, because God loved Israel. Arminian readers see a Gentile giving glory to Israel’s God, the high point of the story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Chronicles describes the throne as God’s throne, while 1 Kings 10:9 speaks of the throne of Israel. Both traditions read the verse as showing that the king’s purpose was to do justice and righteousness for God’s people.

verses.text: She gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold, spices in great abundance, and precious stones. There was never before such spice as the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes: She gives the king a hundred twenty talents of gold, spices in great abundance, and precious stones. Arminians see generous gifts expressing her honor for Solomon and the God who blessed him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the gifts as part of the wealth God brought to Solomon. Both traditions note the parallel with 1 Kings 10:10, and a talent weighed about 66 pounds.

verses.text: The servants of Huram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, also brought algum trees and precious stones.
verses.arminianNotes: Huram’s and Solomon’s servants bring algum trees and precious stones from Ophir. Arminian readers note that 1 Kings 10:11 spells the wood almug, and they read the difference as a variant spelling of the same wood.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference without harmonizing it. Both traditions note that the exact kind of wood is uncertain, possibly a fine-grained, fragrant wood such as sandalwood.

verses.text: The king used algum tree wood to make terraces for the LORD’s house and for the king’s house, and harps and stringed instruments for the singers. There were none like these seen before in the land of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon uses the algum wood for terraces for the LORD’s house and the king’s house, and for harps and stringed instruments for the singers. Arminians note that 1 Kings 10:12 speaks of pillars rather than terraces.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference by reference. Both traditions see the use of fine wood for temple music as showing the care given to worship in Solomon’s reign.

verses.text: King Solomon gave to the queen of Sheba all her desire, whatever she asked, more than that which she had brought to the king. So she turned and went to her own land, she and her servants.
verses.arminianNotes: Solomon gives the queen all her desire, more than she brought, and she returns home. Arminian readers see Solomon’s generosity matching hers, and they note that 1 Kings 10:13 describes his gifts in different words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and name the difference without harmonizing it. Both traditions read the closing of the visit as showing the honor and goodwill that God’s blessing on Solomon brought among the nations.
